Source Basis: RadPrimer-only.
🔍 Key Imaging Findings

  • FNH scar: T2 bright with delayed persistent enhancement on CT or intravascular MR contrast; it does not take up/retain gadoxetate in the illustrated delayed hepatobiliary image.
  • Giant hemangioma: lesions >5 cm commonly have a fibrotic nonenhancing scar that may calcify, while nonscarred portions show typical nodular enhancement.
  • HCC: large heterogeneous hypervascular mass with washout, central necrosis/scar, and rarely calcified scar; vascular invasion and metastases are common.
  • Adenoma: apparent scar-like low-density foci may be fat, necrosis, or old hemorrhage rather than true scar; chemical-shift signal drop supports fat.
  • Metastases: target appearance and central necrosis/fibrosis can mimic scar; mucinous colon or ovarian metastases may calcify.

  • Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma: multiple coalescent peripheral nodules with target/lollipop appearance on CECT or MR and capsular retraction.

  • Central scar plus peripheral nodular enhancement favors giant hemangioma.
  • Large calcified scar in a heterogeneous mass favors fibrolamellar HCC or giant hemangioma; use enhancement pattern and aggressive findings to separate them.
  • Delayed fibrous enhancement with capsular retraction or biliary/portal obstruction favors cholangiocarcinoma.
  • Multiplicity pushes toward metastases, epithelioid hemangioendothelioma, or regenerative nodules when the morphology fits.

Fibrolamellar HCC is a large heterogeneous mass on all phases of imaging. The scar is large and often calcified (>60%). Aggressive signs are present at presentation in more than 60%, including local invasion of vessels/bile ducts and metastases.
Source: RadPrimer, Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar.

column1: Cholangiocarcinoma pattern recall: delayed fibrous scar mimic LMSCH011
column15: What enhancement and associated findings favor mass-forming intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma?
column16:
Focal necrosis or fibrosis may resemble a scar. Extensive fibrous stroma produces typical delayed persistent enhancement. Associated findings include overlying capsular retraction, hepatic volume loss, biliary obstruction, and portal venous obstruction.
Source: RadPrimer, Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar.

column1: EHE pattern recall: peripheral target lollipop lesions LMSCH012
column15: What CT/MR pattern favors hepatic epithelioid hemangioendothelioma?
column16:
Multiple, coalescent, peripheral nodules with target or lollipop appearance on CECT or MR, often with capsular retraction over the lesions.
Key differentiator: peripheral coalescent target/lollipop lesions plus capsular retraction should move EHE above solitary scar-bearing tumors.
Source: RadPrimer, Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar.

column1: NRH pattern recall: Budd-Chiari regenerative scar nodules LMSCH013
column15: What pattern favors nodular regenerative hyperplasia/large regenerative nodules rather than tumor?
column16:
The multiacinar form of nodular regenerative hyperplasia may produce large regenerative nodules with central scars. They are usually multiple, usually <4 cm, and usually occur in patients with Budd-Chiari syndrome.
Source: RadPrimer, Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar.

column1: NRH pattern recall: gadobenate retention LMSCH014
column15: What delayed MR contrast behavior supports regenerative nodules in the illustrated Budd-Chiari cases?
column16:
At 2 hours after IV gadobenate dimeglumine, the nodules show persistent uptake and retention. The caption interprets this as functional hepatocytes with deficient biliary ducts.
Key differentiator: retention supports regenerative/hepatocellular tissue rather than nonhepatocellular metastases.
Source: RadPrimer image captions, Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar.
